paragraphs.text: Lesson 7, considering a career change.
Phil is thinking about changing careers.
Listen to his conversation with Andrew and answer the comprehension questions.
So, how did your interview go?
I think it went pretty well.
They seemed to like me.
Yeah?
That's great.
You were super nervous about it.
I know.
I hate interviews.
I just don't perform well when I'm the center of attention and I have to brag about my skills
and stuff.
It feels unnatural and I always sound awkward.
I'm sure you're being too hard on yourself, but I'm glad it went well.
What did you think about the job?
It sounds like it has potential.
It'd certainly be a step up for my current position.
So if it were just between those two choices, it'd be an easy decision, but I still have to
consider other options.
What do you mean?
Well, I'm toying with the idea of leaving teaching altogether.
Really?
What brought this on?
Well, higher education is just so unstable right now.
College costs a huge chunk of change and there's been a major uptick in online learning.
So who knows what'll happen in the next 10 or 15 years?
Plus, I can earn a lot more in industry.
Yeah, it's important to like your job and everything, but passion doesn't pay the bills.
Do you think your skills could easily transfer from academics to industry?
No, not directly, but having a PhD proves that I'm at least somewhat competent, right?
I don't know, I guess I'm just hoping and praying that companies have a use for someone
with a math brain.
Right.
What areas are you considering?
As far as I can tell, there's currently a demand for data miners and actuaries.
Yeah, I have no clue what those are.
Well, data miners sort through large amounts of information to find patterns, and actuaries
use statistics to assess risk.
For instance, actuaries work for insurance companies to calculate how much they should
charge their clients.
Hmm, it sounds kind of dull.
Tell me about it.
That's what worries me.
What if I make the transition and end up hating it?
I don't want to be stuck in a cubicle all day doing something that just makes me miserable.
And if I leave teaching, it might be really hard to go back.
I don't want to shoot myself in the foot.
Well, good luck with that, buddy.
I'm afraid I don't have any words of wisdom for you.
I'd hate to be in your shoes right now.
Let's learn the vocabulary from Phil and Andrew's conversation.
Phil says he hates interviews because he doesn't perform well when he has to brag about
his skills.
Now, the word brag means to talk about yourself and your accomplishments in an arrogant way.
Bragging is a negative thing.
It's annoying and arrogant.
In a job interview, you don't really have to brag.
You just have to present yourself in a positive way.
But Phil is using the word brag, which has a negative connotation because he just doesn't
like drawing attention to himself.
He says it feels unnatural and I always sound awkward.
The word awkward means strange and socially uncomfortable.
Andrew says I'm sure you're being too hard on yourself.
Being too hard on yourself means demanding too much from yourself, like your standards
for yourself are too high, so you feel like you're not good enough.
Andrew then asks Phil, what do you think about the job?
Phil says it would certainly be a step up from my current position.
A step up means an improvement.
However, Phil is toying with the idea of leaving teaching altogether.
This phrase, toying with the idea means casually considering the idea.
And the word altogether means completely, so Phil is casually thinking about leaving
teaching completely.
Andrew asks, really?
What brought this on?
This question, what brought this on, means what caused this?
Phil replies, well, higher education is just so unstable right now.
The word higher education refers to colleges and universities, education after high school.
Phil says, college costs a huge chunk of change.
A huge chunk of change is slang for a lot of money.
And, he says, there's been a major uptick in online learning.
An uptick is an increase.
Phil says it's important to like your job and everything, but passion doesn't pay the bills.
This expression doesn't pay the bills means it doesn't provide enough money to survive or live.
Andrew asks if Phil's skills could easily transfer from academics to industry.
Phil says, no, not directly, but having a PhD proves that I'm at least somewhat competent, right?
A PhD is a doctorate degree.
Then he says, I don't know, I guess I'm just hoping and praying that companies have a use for someone with a math brain.
This expression, hoping and praying, simply means greatly hoping.
Andrew asks, what areas of industry Phil is considering?
And Phil says, as far as I can tell, there's currently a demand for data miners and actuaries.
The expression, as far as I can tell, means based on the available information.
And Andrew replies, yeah, I have no clue what those are.
The expression, I have no clue, means I have absolutely no idea.
Phil explains, data miners sort through large amounts of information to find patterns.
Patterns are repeating designs or repeating events.
And actuaries use statistics to assess risk.
The word assess means evaluate.
Andrew remarks, it sounds kind of dull.
Dull means boring.
And Phil says, tell me about it.
That means, you're completely correct, or I agree.
Phil is worried that he might end up hating his job.
He says, I don't want to be stuck in a cubicle all day.
A cubicle is a small office area in a larger room.
It's like a box divided from the other office areas by temporary walls.
And Phil adds, if I leave teaching, it might be really hard to go back.
I don't want to shoot myself in the foot.
This idiom, shoot myself in the foot, means accidentally cause damage to myself or my progress.
Andrew wishes him good luck.
He says, I'm afraid I don't have any words of wisdom for you.
Words of wisdom means good advice.
Then he says, I'd hate to be in your shoes right now.
I'd hate to be in your shoes means I would not want to be in your situation.
It's definitely a tough situation, but hopefully Phil will find the right thing to do.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
